Analytical notes, supporting results, and response material for the eLife revision.

**Goal**: compare a covariance-dominated rule with the rate-dominated rule in a setting with multiple competing inhibitory-to-excitatory connections.


## Three neuron motif dynamics {#sec-three-neuron-motif}

![Three-neuron motif with one excitatory neuron and two inhibitory neurons. The diagram labels the excitatory input $h_e$, an excitatory-to-inhibitory connection $W_e$, two inhibitory-to-excitatory connections $W_1$ and $W_2$, inhibitory rates are $r_i$, fixed by an adaptive input.](Attachments/20261005-113251-three_neurons_motif.png){#fig-three-neuron-motif fig-alt="c_1 cyan triangular neuron above two magenta circular neurons. Blue arrows indicate input and an excitatory connection; red dashed connections with terminal dots link both lower neurons to the upper neuron." width=450px}

We consider a simple three-neuron motif, with one excitatory neuron and two inhibitory neurons, modeled as Hawkes processes (@fig-three-neuron-motif). The excitatory neuron receives a constant input $h_e>0$, and projects to one of the inhibitory neurons with a strong weight $W_e$. In this setting inhibitory neuron 1 will have a strong correlation with the excitatory neuron, while inhibitory neuron 2 will be assumed as uncorrelated. The two inhibitory neurons project back to the excitatory neuron with plastic weights $W_1$ and $W_2$. All neurons have an exponential synaptic kernel with timescale $\tau_{\text{syn}}.$ All synaptic weights are assumed positive. An adaptive input ensures that all inhibitory rates are fixed at $r_i$. The excitatory rate can vary over time and is given by:
$$
r_e = h_e - W_1 \,r_i - W_2 \,r_i = h_e - (W_1 + W_2) \,r_i
$$ {#eq-excitatory-rate}

The two inhibitory-to-excitatory synapses $W_1$ and $W_2$ are plastic, following identical symmetric plasticity rules. The average synaptic weight dynamics are given by:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\,W_1}{dt} &= \alpha_{\text{pre}} \,r_i + \alpha_{\text{post}} \,r_e + B \,r_i \,r_e - M^{10}\,W_1\,r_i  + M^{01}\, W_e \, r_e \\
\frac{d\,W_2}{dt} &= \alpha_{\text{pre}} \,r_i + \alpha_{\text{post}} \,r_e + B \,r_i \,r_e - M^{10}\,W_2\,r_i
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-weight-dynamics}
Where $B$ is the area under the STDP curve, and the $M$ terms represent the first-order motif contributions to plasticity (ignoring higher order contributions). Since here we only consider symmetric rules $M^{10} = M^{01} := M$.

In the Vogels-Spreckeler rule we have:
$$
\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{Vog}} = 0, \quad B^{\text{Vog}} = 1
$$ {#eq-vogels-constants}
The $M^{\text{Vog}}$ term is:
$$
M^{\text{Vog}} = \frac{1}{2\,\left(\tau_+ + \tau_{\text{syn}} \right)}
$$ {#eq-vogels-motif}
And $\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{Vog}}$ is a free parameter set to ensure that the rate of the excitatory neuron is maintained at a target value $r_e^{\text{(target)}}$.

In the covariance-dominated rule instead:
$$
 \quad B^{\text{cov}} = 0  ,\quad
M^{\text{cov}} = \frac{1}{2\,\left(\tau_+ + \tau_{\text{syn}} \right)}
-  \frac{1}{2\,\left(\tau_- + \tau_{\text{syn}} \right)}
$$ {#eq-covariance-motif}
And both $\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{cov}}$ and $\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{cov}}$ are free parameters that can be used to set the target rate. Here for simplicity we will set $\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{cov}} = 0$, but all our results hold in the general case (see detailed analytic notes).

For $\tau_- \gg \tau_+$ and $\tau_- \gg \tau_{\text{syn}}$, $M^{\text{Vog}}$ and $M^{\text{cov}}$ are similar. The main difference between the rules is therefore in the $B^{\text{Vog}}=1$ and $B^{\text{cov}}=0$ terms.

### Fixed point solution {#sec-report-fixed-point}

#### General {#sec-report-fixed-point-general}

If the stable fixed-point conditions are fulfilled (see detailed analytic notes), the excitatory rate and weights converge to


$$
\begin{aligned}
r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&= \frac{M\,h_e-2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i}
 {M\,(1+W_e)+2\,(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i)},\\
W_1^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&= \frac{h_e+(W_e-1)\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{2\,r_i}, \\
W_2^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&= \frac{h_e-(1+W_e)\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{2\,r_i}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-report-fixed-point-weights}

Setting the fixed-point rate equal to $r_e^{\text{(target)}}$ requires

$$
\alpha_{\text{pre}}
= -\frac{\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i}{r_i}\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}
 + \frac{M}{2\,r_i}\,
   \left[h_e-(1+W_e)\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}\right].
$$ {#eq-report-target-presynaptic-constant}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Most important result here!

The final weights depend on the plasticity rule parameters only through $r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$. Therefore, any rule that reaches a specific excitatory target rate as a stable fixed point, will also have the same stable final inhibitory weights!!! In this setting the stable solution is rule-invariant, no matter if rate-dominated or covariance dominated, and the only difference between rules is in the dynamics of convergence to the fixed point!

:::


#### Vogels-Sprekeler rule {#sec-report-fixed-point-vogels}

With $\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{Vog}}=0$ and $B^{\text{Vog}}=1$,

$$
r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
= \frac{M^{\text{Vog}}\,h_e-2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{Vog}}\,r_i}
 {M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+W_e)+2\,r_i},
\qquad
\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{Vog}}
= -r_e^{\text{(target)}}
 + \frac{M^{\text{Vog}}}{2\,r_i}\,
   \left[h_e-(1+W_e)\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}\right].
$$ {#eq-report-vogels-target}


#### Covariance-based rule {#sec-report-fixed-point-covariance}

With $\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{cov}}=0$ and $B^{\text{cov}}=0$, assuming
$M^{\text{cov}}>0$ (thus $\tau_->\tau_+$),

$$
r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
= \frac{h_e}{1+W_e}
 - \frac{2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{cov}}\,r_i}
 {M^{\text{cov}}\,(1+W_e)},
\qquad
\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{cov}}
= \frac{M^{\text{cov}}}{2\,r_i}\,
   \left[h_e-(1+W_e)\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}\right].
$$ {#eq-report-covariance-target}

### Convergence of sum and difference modes {#sec-report-convergence-modes}

Although the fixed point is rule-invariant, the convergence dynamics are not. To analyze the convergence dynamics, we define sum and difference modes of the inhibitory weights.

$$
W_s := W_1+W_2,
\qquad
W_d := W_1-W_2.
$$ {#eq-report-mode-definitions}
We use $\tau_s$ and $\tau_d$ to denote the relaxation times of the sum and difference modes, respectively.

The excitatory rate depends only on the sum mode (see equation @eq-excitatory-rate), therefore the convergence of sum mode is equivalent to the convergence of the excitatory rate to $r_e^{\text{(target)}}$. However, a full separation of weights implies that the difference mode has reached convergence.

Let $\eta>0$ be the learning rate multiplying the right-hand side of each
plasticity equation in @eq-weight-dynamics (the equations above use $\eta=1$).
This rescales the convergence times without changing the fixed point.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_s
&= \frac{1}
 {\eta\,r_i\,\left[M\,(1+W_e)+2\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+2\,B\,r_i\right]}, \\
\tau_d
&= \frac{1}{\eta\,M\,r_i}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-report-mode-timescales}

The ratio of the sum-mode timescale to the difference-mode timescale is

$$
\frac{\tau_s}{\tau_d}
= \frac{M}{M\,(1+W_e)+2\,(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i)}.
$$ {#eq-report-mode-timescale-ratio}

Since the sum drives the difference through $r_e$, the difference generally contains both timescales.

#### Vogels-Sprekeler rule {#sec-report-timescales-vogels}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_s^{\text{Vog}}
&= \frac{1}
 {\eta^{\text{Vog}}\,r_i\,\left[M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+W_e)+2\,r_i\right]}, \\
\tau_d^{\text{Vog}}
&= \frac{1}{\eta^{\text{Vog}}\,M^{\text{Vog}}\,r_i}.\\
\frac{\tau_s^{\text{Vog}}}{\tau_d^{\text{Vog}}}
&= \frac{M^{\text{Vog}}}
 {M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+W_e)+2\,r_i}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-report-vogels-timescale-ratio}

For $M^{\text{Vog}}\ll2\,r_i$, expanding gives

$$
\frac{\tau_s^{\text{Vog}}}{\tau_d^{\text{Vog}}}
= \frac{M^{\text{Vog}}}{2\,r_i}
 - \frac{(1+W_e)\,(M^{\text{Vog}})^2}{4\,r_i^2}
 + \mathcal{O}\!\left((M^{\text{Vog}})^3\right).
$$ {#eq-report-vogels-inverse-ratio-small-m}

Therefore $\tau_s \ll \tau_d$ , the sum relaxes much faster than the difference in this regime.

#### Covariance-based rule {#sec-report-timescales-covariance}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_s^{\text{cov}}
&= \frac{1}
 {\eta^{\text{cov}}\,M^{\text{cov}}\,r_i\,(1+W_e)}, \\
\tau_d^{\text{cov}}
&= \frac{1}{\eta^{\text{cov}}\,M^{\text{cov}}\,r_i}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-report-covariance-timescales}

$$
\frac{\tau_s^{\text{cov}}}{\tau_d^{\text{cov}}}
= \frac{1}{1+W_e}.
$$ {#eq-report-covariance-timescale-ratio}

This ratio is independent of $M^{\text{cov}}$ and in our parameter range $\mathcal{O}(1)$.

#### Matching the sum-mode timescales {#sec-report-matched-sum-timescales}

For the same $r_i$ and $W_e$, imposing
$\tau_s^{\text{Vog}}=\tau_s^{\text{cov}}$ requires

$$
\frac{\eta^{\text{Vog}}}{\eta^{\text{cov}}}
= \frac{M^{\text{cov}}\,(1+W_e)}
 {M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+W_e)+2\,r_i}.
$$ {#eq-report-matched-learning-rates}

## Numerical simulations {#sec-report-numerical-simulations}

### Different learning rates {#sec-report-different-learning-rates}

| Rate-dominated | 0.0513 | 1.389 | $1/27.1 \approx 0.037$ |

## Conclusions

Although the fixed point is rule-invariant, in the Vogels-Sprekeler rule the sum mode relaxes much faster than the difference mode, while in the covariance-dominated rule the two modes relax on similar timescales. Therefore, the covariance-dominated rule is more effective at separating inhibitory weights, and existing work based on Vogels-Sprekeler might simply ignore or underestimate this very slow adaptation, "masking" is under other effects and variations.

See for example the plot below from [Lagzi & Fairhall (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adi4350), based on the Vogels-Sprekeler rule, where the simulation is interrupted much earlier than convergence is reached.

![Average inhibitory postsynaptic potential over time for two inhibitory populations, with simulation traces in blue and theoretical curves in black.
